📌 Hidden Fees: Why “Zero Fee” Doesn’t Mean Free

Main Points
⏺ Crypto trade costs can hide in spreads, slippage, and execution routes
⏺ “No fee” often means the cost moves somewhere else
⏺ This post explains how to see the real price of an action

1️⃣ Spread — the gap between buy and sell price can already be your first hidden cost.
2️⃣ Slippage — weaker liquidity pushes your final price away from the quote.
3️⃣ Routing — an app or aggregator may choose a route that benefits it more than you.
4️⃣ Network Costs — even if the platform charges no fee, gas is still a real expense.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — compare final received amounts, check multiple routes, and don’t trust “0% fee” alone.

Final Thoughts

Trades are rarely free. If the fee isn’t visible in one line, it may live inside price, routing, or liquidity.

German investigators have focused on a group of Ukrainian nationals suspected of using a rented sailing yacht, the Andromeda, to transport an operational team into the Baltic Sea.

Investigative reporting has described evidence including traces of explosives and other material potentially linking the vessel to the suspected operation. 

German prosecutors have pursued the case against alleged participants, but the existence of a suspected team does not, by itself, establish who authorized the mission.

Schröm’s investigation also attributes important roles to Ukrainian intelligence and military figures. He has alleged that former Ukrainian military intelligence chief Vasyl Burba and former intelligence officer Roman Chervinsky were involved in organizing the operation. 

He has further claimed that former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi knew about and approved the plan, while Zelensky was not informed.These allegations remain contested and require independent corroboration. 

The involvement of Ukrainian nationals would not automatically prove that the Ukrainian government ordered the attack, just as evidence of prior American intelligence knowledge would not automatically prove that Washington directed it.

Three voices, three different perspectivesThe public record offers sharply contrasting assessments of the mystery. 

An intelligence source quoted by NOS and Nieuwsuur in June 2023 warned of the political implications of the case: “I suspect that the outcome of the investigation is an inconvenient truth.”

Zelensky, responding to allegations of Ukrainian involvement, offered a direct denial: “I believe that our army and our intelligence services knew nothing about it.”

The German government, meanwhile, has emphasized the importance of the criminal investigation over speculation in the media, maintaining that responsibility must be established through evidence and proper legal proceedings.

The statements carry different evidentiary weight. An anonymous intelligence source can offer insight but cannot independently establish responsibility. A political leader’s denial is relevant but does not settle the facts. And a government’s insistence on due process underscores how much remains unresolved.

What did Washington really know? The CIA has not publicly confirmed the specific allegations that it offered financial support to the alleged organizers. Earlier reporting documented an American warning to Ukraine after Dutch intelligence obtained information about a possible operation, but that reporting does not independently establish that the CIA supported the eventual sabotage.

The distinction could prove decisive. If investigators uncover communications or financial records showing that American officials offered assistance, the implications would extend far beyond the destruction of a pipeline. 

The findings could trigger questions about intelligence oversight, the obligations of allies and the limits of covert operations during wartime.

If the evidence instead shows that American intelligence learned of the plan and attempted to stop it, the central issue would be whether the warnings were timely, effective and communicated to the right people. 

For Germany, the stakes remain enormous. For the United States, the allegations touch on the credibility of intelligence cooperation with European allies. For Ukraine, they raise questions about the boundaries between military necessity, covert action and political accountability.

The Baltic Sea has already revealed the physical consequences of the explosions. What remains hidden is the chain of decisions that preceded them.

Until those questions are answered with independently verified evidence, the Nord Stream case remains one of Europe’s most consequential unresolved sabotage investigations — a story of underwater explosions, secret warnings and decisions that may have been made long before the first blast shook the Baltic Sea.

🔖 Australia proposes new crypto exchange rules for 2027 

📣 Australia has proposed new rules for cryptocurrency trading and custody platforms on October 15, 2026, with financial regulator ASIC seeking public feedback by November 27 before the country’s digital asset licensing framework takes effect in April 2027. 

📊 The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) announced the consultation alongside Consultation Paper 392, which outlines planned requirements for customer asset protection, trading practices and financial resources. The regulator expects to publish final guidance in March 2027, giving businesses time to prepare for the new licensing requirements. Australia’s upcoming rules will bring more cryptocurrency businesses under the country’s existing financial services licensing framework.

⚡️ The Corporations Amendment (Digital Assets Framework) Act 2026 creates two regulated categories: digital asset platforms and tokenized custody platforms. Digital asset platforms hold digital tokens for customers and provide related services, while tokenized custody platforms use digital tokens to record customers’ rights to underlying assets.
